To our students, please trust in your preparation. You have worked hard for this. Do not jeopardise your future by attempting to cheat. To school heads and invigilators, you have a duty to uphold fairness and discipline throughout the examination period. WAEC and the Ghana Education Service must intensify supervision, sensitisation and enforcement of sanctions where necessary to safeguard the credibility of this critical academic milestone, which they are doing anyway. Mr Speaker, education is not only a personal journey, it is a constitutional right. Article 38 (2) of the 1992 71 13th June, 2025 72 Statements Constitution charges government to ensure access to free universal basic education. As such, this House must reaffirm its commitment to strengthening infrastructure and teaching resources, expanding training and ethical oversight for educators, investing in digital and inclusive education delivery and improving student support systems, especially in the era of artificial intelligence. Mr Speaker, as our sons and daughters prepare or are already writing this B.E.C.E., let us rally behind them with encouragement and unwavering support. Let us also send strong messages that malpractice has no place in our examination halls. Their success is not only personal; it is the building blocks in the foundation of the future of Ghana. I wish all candidates the very best. May their efforts be rewarded with success and may they continue to raise their honesty, determination and excellence. Mr Speaker, as a result of that, the Government then introduced the licensure examination — Dr Forson — rose — Mr Speaker: Just a minute, Dr Armah. Yes, Hon Minority Leader? Dr Forson: Mr Speaker, the Hon Member quoted and made reference to a law that has been repealed by this House. Mr Speaker, he made reference to the Education Act, 2008 (Act 778). I do not know where he is getting his facts from. However, the reference he has made has clearly been repealed. Mr Speaker, on that basis, you have to rule him out. [Interruption] I did not hear him state that. He did not say that. It has been repealed completely. So, I do not know what he is talking about. Mr Speaker, secondly, the Act talks about certificates and not licensure examinations. That is not what the Act talks about. It has been repealed, in any case. Mr Speaker: Hon Minority Leader, he actually stated that it has been repealed but it has been repeated in the new Act that he read. So he said it has been repealed. Dr Armah: Mr Speaker, I thank you very much. Mr Speaker, I introduced that to buttress the point that in the year 2016 when the then Government said that they were going to introduce the licensure regime, the prevailing Act was the Education Act, 2008 (Act 778), and that Act imposed a statutory requirement for teachers to write that licensure examination. So, it could not be the case that they were going to introduce that without the licensure examination. That is why I said that amounted to double standards. Mr Speaker, let me indicate that the entire process is to improve teacher quality. As we speak now, the qualification of Ghanaian teachers has now received international acceptance. When I left the shores of Ghana to go and teach in the United Kingdom (UK), I went through a serious and laborious assessment process. Mr Speaker, as we speak now, because of the licensure regime — The Ghana Teacher and Licensure Examination and Certification, when a Ghanaian teacher moves to the UK now, they are automatically granted Qualified Teacher Status (QTS), which was very difficult to get then. Mr Speaker, this examination is all part of that full package. So, any attempt to try and scrap it would adulterate the quality that has been accepted internationally. Mr Speaker, having said that, if one looks at the Budget Statement, it is very clear about the support structures that are being given to teachers. So, the fact that people were properly invigilated or they were not allowed to cheat is untenable. In fact, it even goes to confirm that probably there was more cheating in these exams than has been done in the past, if we are looking at the data. But we have been told that WAEC is going to meet the Committee, and then we can have a better interrogation into this matter. Mr Speaker, when we go further, we realise that the Ministry’s commitment, as far as basic education is concerned, cannot be assured. Why? Because, the textbook that was supposed to have been printed in 2025 is the same thing that has been lifted and placed in 2026 Budget. So, where is the trust and the credibility here if we keep repeating the same thing? Mr Speaker, one thing that has been put in this 2026 Budget that is going to kill the private sector is the insistence that the formal Assembly Press should be mandated to print these textbooks. Whether they have the capacity, I do not have a problem, but we are in a competitive country where we expect the private sector to create jobs. Unfortunately, this Budget is going to kill the private sector. About GH₵564 million is being given to one company. Where is the fairness here? Where is the transparency? It has to be competitive. We should allow the private sector to be able to participate so that they can create more jobs. We want jobs for our youth. Already, people have been sacked at the beginning of 2025, while we are trying to kill the private sector that they cannot create jobs. If this is made competitive, then, of course, we will be able to print these textbooks and improve on performance. Mr Speaker, one other reason why we realise that the performance of our students was very poor is the fact that the Minister for Education, on the 25th of June, stood in this House and stated categorically that we are going to employ 50,000 instructors to support education. Unfortunately, nothing happened. So, if we intend to support education and to improve on the human capital of this country, then we have to walk the talk. We cannot just be putting figures for nothing, but rather we should make sure that everything that we put in for education—That is the base of our development and everything we do—We expect that when this Budget is approved for the Ministry, it will be released for the them to work. Another important thing is the fact that most agencies across all the ministries we have met, do not have the opportunity to utilise their allocation for CAPEX or goods and services because of commitment authorisation.
